content: Vin Mariani, also known as Mariani's wine, was a tonic created around 1863 by Angelo Mariani, a French chemist. Mariani became fascinated with coca and its economic potential after reading a paper by Paolo Mantegazza on the effects of coca. In 1863, he began marketing a wine called Vin Mariani, which was made by infusing Bordeaux wine with coca leaves. The ethanol in the wine acted as a solvent, extracting cocaine from the coca leaves and altering the drink's effects. The tonic contained approximately 2 mg of cocaine per ounce, a concentration designed to compete with similar beverages in the United States that had higher cocaine content. In 1884, John S. Pemberton created a similar coca wine called Pemberton's French Wine Coca, inspired by Vin Mariani. However, in 1885, when Atlanta and Fulton County passed prohibition laws, Pemberton developed Coca-Cola as a non-alcoholic, carbonated version of Mariani's wine. This new beverage included the addition of kola nuts, which provided caffeine, and retained coca leaves as a stimulant. The name Coca-Cola reflected these two key ingredients. Angelo Mariani is sometimes referred to as the grandfather of Coca-Cola due to his influence on the beverage's creation. When cocaine is consumed alone, it produces two primary active compounds: benzoylecgonine and ecgonine methyl ester. However, when combined with alcohol, as in Vin Mariani, the mixture forms cocaethylene, a potent psychoactive compound. Cocaethylene is more euphoric than cocaine alone but also has greater cardiovascular toxicity. Vin Mariani was highly popular during its time, attracting notable figures, including royalty such as Queen Victoria of Great Britain and Ireland. Pope Leo XIII and later Pope Saint Pius X were also known to be drinkers of Vin Mariani. Pope Leo XIII even awarded the wine a Vatican gold medal and appeared on a poster endorsing it. Recently, a group of UK investors under the name Mariani Amalgamated Ltd has revived the production of Vin Mariani.
